# Is it safe to get power from OBD 2 port for dash cam?

When selecting a power source for an in-dash camera, the immediate technical constraint is battery capacity versus thermal safety. Most standard portable power banks lack sufficient watt-hour (Wh) density to sustain hours of recording while the vehicle is completely off without generating excessive heat or draining prematurely. While leaving a high-capacity lithium-ion bank inside a cabin exposed to direct sunlight poses genuine fire risks due to uncontrolled thermal runaway, the OBD-II port presents a fundamentally different power delivery profile that warrants closer inspection for safety and reliability.

The primary concern with generic OBD-to-USB adapters found on marketplaces like Amazon is often the quality of the isolation transformer and voltage regulation circuitry. However, from an electrical engineering perspective, tapping into the OBD-II interface carries inherent risks if not handled correctly. The OBD-II standard defines pin 16 as the dedicated "Battery" supply, which should theoretically be isolated from the vehicle's ignition switch logic to ensure continuous power even when the car is off.

If you inspect the wiring harness of a compliant OBD-II adapter, you will see it connects directly to these pins. The critical safety feature here is that pin 16 is fused and regulated by the vehicle manufacturer specifically for aftermarket accessories like dash cams. In contrast, plugging into pin 4 (ACC) or pin 5 (IGN) cuts power immediately when the key turns off, defeating the purpose of parking mode recording unless you are relying on a hardwired cut-off relay logic inside your own device.

A safer alternative to generic USB adapters involves utilizing the OBD-II port via a vehicle's diagnostic interface rather than an external brick. Many modern vehicles support direct CAN bus communication or specific power taps that can be accessed without drawing from the main battery through a cheap adapter. For developers comfortable with custom electronics, reading the pinout and verifying continuity on pins 16 (Battery), 4 (ACC), and 5 (IGN) before soldering connections is essential.

One common pitfall in this setup is the lack of reverse polarity protection. If an unregulated OBD adapter fails internally or if the vehicle's battery voltage spikes during cold cranking, a poorly designed USB adapter might feed that surge back into your dash cam's charging port, potentially frying its internal regulator. A robust solution requires checking for built-in fuse holders on the OBD side of these adapters; many reputable brands include a 2A inline fuse specifically to protect against shorts in the data cables or power banks.

Another consideration is the ground loop issue. Some vehicles utilize the chassis as a return path, while others strictly use wire-to-wire connections for CAN bus signals. If your dash cam's USB power cable introduces a ground reference that conflicts with the vehicle's signal grounds, you may experience intermittent disconnections or noise on video feeds. This often manifests as dropped frames during long parking sessions when static electricity builds up in the cabin.

Ultimately, relying on a cheap, unbranded OBD-to-USB adapter is risky because the isolation quality cannot be verified without opening the casing to inspect the transformer and capacitors. A more reliable approach is to use an adapter from a reputable manufacturer that explicitly certifies compliance with automotive electrical standards, ensuring proper fuse protection and voltage clamping. If you are already managing complex vehicle integrations for other projects, understanding these power dynamics becomes even more critical when dealing with sensitive embedded systems that cannot tolerate brownouts or noise.
